answers.answer: In SCOPe 2.08 all three are placed in the same superfamily, b.6.1 Cupredoxins (sunid 49503), within fold b.6 Cupredoxin-like (sunid 49502), class b (all beta). Each is a separate FAMILY: plastocyanin/azurin-like is b.6.1.1 (sunid 49504), ephrin ectodomain is b.6.1.5 (sunid 74874; e.g. ephrin-B2 ectodomain, ephrin-A5, d1ikop_) and PAD4 N-terminal domain is b.6.1.6 (sunid 110107; e.g. d5n0ya1, d5n0ma1). So SCOPe treats them as distant evolutionary relatives (shared superfamily, i.e. a common-ancestry/homology call based on structure and weak sequence/feature evidence). That is a weaker relationship than same-family, which would imply clear sequence-level relatedness and usually conserved function. Their different families mean they are not close homologs; they share a Greek-key beta-sandwich (cupredoxin-like) scaffold and little else. The superfamily node's only annotation is 'contains copper-binding site' (b.6.1 level). That describes the superfamily as a whole, mainly the classic cupredoxin families. It is not a per-family guarantee. Sibling families in b.6.1 are quite different: the cytochrome c oxidase subunit II periplasmic domain (b.6.1.2, CuA site), multidomain cupredoxins (b.6.1.3), nitrosocyanin (b.6.1.4), and SO1698-like (b.6.1.7), and not all carry a copper site or do electron transfer. Inference: copper binding and electron transfer should NOT be transferred from plastocyanin/azurin to ephrin ectodomains or the PAD4 N-terminal domain. Ephrin ectodomains are cell-surface ligand/receptor-binding domains (Eph receptor recognition, in SCOPe the receptor ligand-binding domain is in an unrelated b.18.1 fold), with no copper-site role. PAD4's N-terminal domain is part of a calcium-dependent peptidylarginine deiminase (catalytic domain separately classified d.126.1.5; middle domain b.2.9.1), and its activity is calcium-dependent hydrolysis (citrullination), not redox. A shared fold or distant superfamily membership supports at most a structural-scaffold similarity, not conservation of metal-binding residues (the ligand set His/Cys/His/Met), the type-1 copper site geometry, redox potential, or partner interactions. Function should be supported by conserved active-site/ligand residues, metal-binding evidence (structure, spectroscopy, or ligand/heterogen records), and family-level homology, none of which SCOPe's superfamily grouping provides for these two families. Limits: this is a release-2.08 classification; fold/superfamily labels are structural/evolutionary groupings and not functional annotation; the superfamily comment does not establish copper binding for every member. To go further, one would check metal heterogens in the individual PDB entries (e.g. 5n0y, 5n0m for PAD4, which bind calcium) and sequence-motif conservation.
